title: SlabVault graded-slab consignment comp-cards: neutralize six mixed-light slab photos to an in-frame grey card, hold one consistent fill-scale onto clean white, triage-prep the two grading-partner seals, then data-merge one press-ready comp-card per slab

source.reference: Shopify / collectibles product photo editor — graded-card cutout, white background & consignment cards

grounding_note: Adapted from a real Upwork collectibles-store brief (an online graded sports-card shop wanting iPhone product photos cut out, centered on clean white, resized for its storefront, and named to Shopify handles) and laundered to a fictional client, 'SlabVault Cards'. No real person, shop, athlete, team, card set, or grading company is named anywhere: the two grading partners are the invented fictional companies 'GRADEX' and 'APEX' (never PSA/BGS/SGC/CGC or any real grader), the player and set names on the slabs are invented, and Shopify / Upwork appear only as platform references, not as brands in the scene. REPOSITIONED to remove the killed original's two defects: (1) the old task was one 5-call cutout recipe run six times with NO adaptive reasoning, and (2) its inputs were explicitly generated clean and de-cluttered under even daylight, engineering away the one genuinely hard part (holding a consistent look across differently-lit sources). The corrected job supplies six raw slab photos shot at the kitchen table across two different times of day under mismatched light — each with a photographic 18% grey card laid in frame — so the real, human-hard work is cross-asset neutralization to one shared white point plus a numeric consistent-fill / print-DPI gate, not a repeated cutout. The endpoint is upgraded from a bare folder of white-background squares (asset prep, which the audit flagged as not an owned designed artifact) to a genuine data-merge: the client supplies a hand-authored InDesign single-record consignment comp-card template (.indd) carrying live <<fields>> AND TWO @-prefixed image-path columns (the neutralized slab packshot and the grading-partner seal), plus a consignment roster CSV; document_merge_data_layout emits exactly ONE comp-card per slab (page-count = row-count). The two grading-partner seals are a deliberate two-way triage — one is a flat printed logo seal that can become clean vector line art, the other is a photograph of a holographic tamper-proof authentication hologram that would be destroyed by a trace and must instead be knocked to transparency and kept as high-resolution raster.
one_line_ask: Bring six graded-slab photos shot under mismatched kitchen light to one consistent, true-colour storefront look by neutralizing each to the 18% grey card it carries — deciding per frame how far and which way to move white balance and exposure — then lift each slab onto clean pure-white at ONE consistent fill-scale and print size, prep the two grading-partner seals each the correct way (a flat printed seal is not the same problem as a photographed holographic hologram), and data-merge the client's authored single-record InDesign comp-card template against the consignment roster to produce one press-ready comp-card per slab.
full_brief: SlabVault Cards runs an online consignment storefront for graded sports-card slabs, and we need this new-intake batch turned into a clean, uniform set plus a printed consignment comp-card for each slab. Here is the honest situation with the photos: the owner shot all six slabs on an iPhone at the kitchen table, but across two sittings — a few in the morning by the window (they come out cold and slightly blue), the rest that evening under the warm work-lamp (they come out orange), and one under the greenish overhead in the back room. So straight out of the folder the six look like they were shot by three different people: the same white slab case reads blue in one and amber in another, some are dull and underexposed, one is a touch blown out. A storefront grid where every slab has a different colour cast looks amateur and kills buyer trust on items worth real money. To give you an honest reference we laid a photographic 18% grey card at the edge of every shot. What we need on the photos: bring all six to one consistent, true look by neutralizing each frame to the grey card it contains, so once every card reads a clean neutral the whole set sits at one shared white point and one exposure feel. Do NOT push one blanket correction across all six — each sitting was lit differently and some frames need warming while others need cooling, and forcing the same numbers through all of them will leave the set mismatched. When you are done, tell us the final white-balance and exposure move you landed on for each frame so we can trust the set is genuinely matched and not just eyeballed. Then lift each slab cleanly off the cluttered table — the wood grain, the charger cable, the coffee ring and the grey card must all be gone — and set it on flat pure-white (#FFFFFF), no drop shadow, no grey gradient, just clean white the way the storefront wants. This part has a hard consistency rule the last freelancer missed: every slab must sit at the SAME scale in its frame with even margin, so a small vintage slab and a tall modern slab do not jump size-to-size down the grid; and each finished slab image has to carry enough real pixels to print sharp inside the comp-card photo window — a slab cropped down to a little web thumbnail will print soft and we will reject it. Second, the grading-partner seals: two of our graders' marks go on the cards depending on who graded the slab — the GRADEX seal is a flat printed two-colour logo, and the APEX seal is a photograph of the graders' holographic tamper-proof authentication hologram, all sheen and rainbow gradient. Both need to be prepped so they drop cleanly into the card's seal window and stay sharp at print size — but they are not the same kind of file and should not be handled the same way; think about which one can honestly become clean line art and which one cannot survive that. Finally, build the cards: we have hand-built the InDesign consignment comp-card template with the real placeholder fields and two image slots (the slab photo and the grading seal), and we are giving you the consignment roster; merge them so every slab gets its own single comp-card with the player, set/year, grade, cert number and ask price bound in verbatim from the roster, its cleaned slab photo dropped into the photo window, and its grading-partner seal in the seal window — then hand back a press-ready ~300 DPI PDF, one comp-card per slab. Do not invent or reassign any slab's details; bind them verbatim. Acceptance: every grey card neutral and the whole set on one white point (with your per-frame WB/exposure move reported); every slab on flat pure-white at one consistent fill-scale with even margin and enough resolution to print >=300 DPI in the photo window; the two grading seals each prepped the correct way and razor-sharp at print size; and exactly one finished comp-card per roster row.

inputs.name: slab01_gradex10_modern_rookie.jpg
inputs.gen_prompt: A modern baseball rookie trading card sealed in a clear hard-plastic grading slab; the slab's top label reads 'GRADEX  GEM-MT 10' in red on white with a fictional player name and a fictional cert number, the rookie card clearly visible and readable, resting slightly tilted on a busy wood-grain kitchen table with a phone charger cable and a faint coffee ring in frame. A photographic 18% neutral grey card and a small white swatch lie flat on the table at the lower-left edge of the frame. Shot on an iPhone under COOL blue-cyan window light with a distinct cold cast and a slightly flat, marginally under-exposed exposure. Real plastic-case glare, real wood grain, natural clutter. It is a REAL PHOTOGRAPH, not an illustration or 3D render. Any grading label shows only a FICTIONAL grading company (GRADEX / APEX), never a real brand. Rendered large, roughly 3500 x 4600 px, so the slab can be cropped and downscaled and still clear the print pixel floor.
inputs.realism_notes: SL-01, morning window sitting (COOL/blue, flat). Grey card in frame is the neutralisation target. Deliberately cluttered mixed-light source (the killed original engineered this away) so cutout + per-frame neutralisation + consistent-scale-on-white has genuine work. Rendered oversized so the correct downscale to the >=709 x 992 px comp-card photo window never upscales. Graded by GRADEX -> resolves to the flat vector seal.

inputs.name: slab02_gradex9_vintage.jpg
inputs.gen_prompt: A 1970s-style vintage baseball trading card sealed in a clear grading slab, label reading 'GRADEX  NM-MT 9' with a fictional player name and cert number, the vintage card clearly visible, lying on a cluttered wood kitchen table with a charger cable and coffee-cup ring nearby. A photographic 18% neutral grey card and a white swatch sit at the lower-right edge of the frame. Shot on an iPhone under WARM tungsten work-lamp light with a strong orange cast and slightly under-exposed, dull shadows. Real slab glare and wood grain, natural clutter. A REAL PHOTOGRAPH, not an illustration or render. Grading label is the FICTIONAL company GRADEX only. Rendered roughly 3500 x 4600 px.
inputs.realism_notes: SL-02, evening lamp sitting (WARM/orange, dark). Must move the OPPOSITE direction from SL-01 (cool it, lift exposure) to land on the shared white point -- proves a blanket 'warm everything' pass fails. This is the smallest physical slab in the set, so its consistent-fill-scale crop is a genuine decision. Graded by GRADEX -> flat vector seal.

inputs.name: slab03_gradex95_chrome.jpg
inputs.gen_prompt: A shiny chrome-refractor basketball trading card sealed in a grading slab, label reading 'GRADEX  MINT 9.5' with a fictional player name and cert number and four small subgrade numbers, the colourful refractor card sharp and visible, on a cluttered wood table with a charger and coffee ring. A photographic 18% neutral grey card and a white swatch sit at the frame edge. Shot on an iPhone under GREENISH fluorescent back-room overhead light with a clear green cast AND noticeably under-exposed. Real chrome glare and refractor rainbow sheen, real clutter. A REAL PHOTOGRAPH, not a render. Grading label is FICTIONAL GRADEX only. Rendered roughly 3500 x 4600 px.
inputs.realism_notes: SL-03, back-room sitting (GREEN cast + dark). A two-axis problem: the dominant move is on TINT (push toward magenta to kill green) PLUS a real exposure lift, not a simple temperature slide -- so per-frame reasoning is forced. The reflective chrome refractor also stresses the clean cutout. Graded by GRADEX -> flat vector seal.

inputs.name: slab04_apex9_refractor.jpg
inputs.gen_prompt: A colourful refractor football trading card sealed in a grading slab, black label reading 'APEX  9' with a fictional player name and cert number, the card sharp and visible, on a wood kitchen table with light clutter. A photographic 18% neutral grey card and a white swatch sit at the frame edge. Shot on an iPhone under bright near-daylight that is slightly OVER-EXPOSED, with hot specular highlights blowing out on the top of the plastic case. Real slab sheen, real clutter. A REAL PHOTOGRAPH, not a render. Grading label is the FICTIONAL company APEX only. Rendered roughly 3500 x 4600 px.
inputs.realism_notes: SL-04, over-exposed sitting. Tonal recovery dominates: PULL exposure/highlights/whites down to recover the blown case first, then only a small WB nudge to land the grey card neutral -- the opposite tonal problem to the dark frames. Graded by APEX -> resolves to the holographic RASTER seal (triage).

inputs.name: slab05_apex85_vintage.jpg
inputs.gen_prompt: A vintage basketball trading card sealed in a grading slab, black label reading 'APEX  8.5' with a fictional player name and cert number, the card visible, on a cluttered wood table with a charger cable in frame. A photographic 18% neutral grey card and a white swatch sit at the frame edge. Shot on an iPhone under STRONG cool blue open-shade light AND clearly DARK / under-exposed, so the slab muddies toward shadow. Real slab glare, real clutter. A REAL PHOTOGRAPH, not a render. Grading label is FICTIONAL APEX only. Rendered roughly 3500 x 4600 px.
inputs.realism_notes: SL-05, deep-shade sitting (strong COOL + dark). The BIGGEST correction in the set: warm strongly and lift shadows/exposure to bring it up to the shared white point while protecting the card face from going muddy -- direct proof that identical batch numbers cannot serve every frame. Graded by APEX -> holographic RASTER seal (triage).

inputs.name: slab06_gradex10_hockey_rookie.jpg
inputs.gen_prompt: A modern hockey rookie trading card sealed in a grading slab, label reading 'GRADEX  GEM-MT 10' with a fictional player name and cert number, the card sharp and visible, on a wood kitchen table with faint clutter. A photographic 18% neutral grey card and a white swatch sit at the frame edge. Shot on an iPhone under nearly neutral light that is only slightly WARM and dull / low-contrast. Real slab sheen, light clutter. A REAL PHOTOGRAPH, not a render. Grading label is FICTIONAL GRADEX only. Rendered roughly 3500 x 4600 px.
inputs.realism_notes: SL-06, near-neutral sitting. RESTRAINT case: its grey card is already close to neutral, so only a small WB nudge is needed -- over-correcting pushes it off the set; the real work here is a modest tonal lift (contrast/clarity) to match the set's feel. This is the tallest modern slab, so its consistent-fill-scale crop must match the small vintage SL-02. Graded by GRADEX -> flat vector seal.

inputs.name: gradex_seal_flat.png
inputs.gen_prompt: A flat two-colour printed grading-partner seal reading 'GRADEX  CERTIFIED' -- solid deep-ink lettering and a simple shield emblem on a solid single-colour block, high contrast, hard clean edges, no gradients, no sheen, no photographic texture, exported slightly oversized and off-centre with a thin margin. Looks like printable line art / a logo file. Fictional company GRADEX only.
inputs.realism_notes: One of the two grading seals -- flat, high-contrast, solid-fill, so image_vectorize yields a clean SVG after prep-before-trace (crop-to-bounds + crisp). The seal that CAN honestly become clean vector line art.

inputs.name: apex_seal_holo.png
inputs.gen_prompt: A close-up PHOTOGRAPH of a printed holographic tamper-proof authentication hologram reading 'APEX' on a dark surface: a shiny metallic rainbow-gradient foil with specular highlights, reflections, subtle surface texture and smooth colour transitions across the letters and background. Clearly a photographed glossy holographic object, not flat line art -- full of gradients and sheen. Fictional company APEX only.
inputs.realism_notes: THE TRIAGE / TRAP asset. It looks like 'just another grading seal', but it is a photographed holographic surface full of gradients and specular sheen: feeding it to image_vectorize returns a flat, muddy silhouette that destroys the hologram. The correct treatment is crop-to-bounds -> image_remove_background to transparency -> keep as high-resolution raster placed via @Seal. Getting it wrong is invisible in a thumbnail and only shows when the APEX cards print flat and dead.

inputs.name: slabvault_compcard.indd
inputs.gen_prompt: AUTHORED DELIVERABLE (cannot be model-generated): a genuine, hand-built Adobe InDesign document (.indd/.idml) for a SINGLE-RECORD 89 x 127 mm portrait consignment comp-card with 3 mm bleed -- ONE slab per page. It must contain live InDesign data-merge placeholder fields <<PlayerName>>, <<SetYear>>, <<Grade>>, <<CertNo>>, <<AskPrice>>, and TWO @-prefixed image-path merge columns wired to two separate image frames: a 60 x 84 mm portrait photo window bound to @Packshot, and a 24 x 24 mm square seal window bound to @Seal. The <<PlayerName>> text frame has Auto-Size 'shrink text to fit' enabled so long player names bind without going overset. The SlabVault masthead, the consignment terms line and the price band are already drawn into the template artwork (fixed on every card), so the only per-row imagery is the slab photo and the grading seal. Built by hand in InDesign so the merge fields and BOTH image fields actually bind. Explicitly NOT a convert_pdf_to_indd output: a converted-PDF template has no live merge fields and no data-merge image field, so it would not bind -- which is exactly the defect this rebuild avoids.
inputs.realism_notes: document_merge_data_layout is [T] and REQUIRES a user-authored .indd carrying real merge fields plus genuine @image-path columns, and it emits ONE FILE PER ROW -- so a single-record per-slab comp-card is the correct, connector-doable shape (one card per slab), not a multi-up sheet. Supplied as an input, not a chain output. Two image columns (@Packshot, @Seal) mean the merge must resolve two prepped assets per row. Column names must exactly match the roster headers. Text-only document_merge_data_vector is the WRONG tool here because it cannot bind an image column.

inputs.name: slabvault_consignment_roster.csv
inputs.gen_prompt: Generate a CSV with headers exactly: PlayerName,SetYear,Grade,CertNo,AskPrice,@Packshot,@Seal and 6 rows (one per slab, in the order slab01..slab06). PlayerName is a mix of fictional player names including at least two DELIBERATELY LONG names (e.g. 'Emmanuel Vandersteldt-Okonkwo') alongside short ones so the template's shrink-to-fit is exercised. SetYear is a fictional set + year string. Grade maps to the label on each slab (GRADEX GEM-MT 10, GRADEX NM-MT 9, GRADEX MINT 9.5, APEX 9, APEX 8.5, GRADEX GEM-MT 10). CertNo is a fictional cert number. AskPrice is a dollar amount. @Packshot holds the agreed prepped packshot filename in row order (packshot_sl01_final.jpg ... packshot_sl06_final.jpg). @Seal maps from the grading company on each slab: GRADEX rows -> gradex_seal.svg, APEX rows -> apex_seal.png (so rows 4 and 5 resolve to the holographic raster and the other four to the flat vector). Column names must exactly match the template merge fields and the two @image-path columns.
inputs.realism_notes: Six rows => the merge must produce exactly six finished comp-cards (page-count = row-count gate). The @Packshot / @Seal columns hold the filenames the agent must produce and upload under those exact names, so naming discipline is a real dependency. The grading-company -> @Seal mapping means the APEX rows resolve to the holographic raster while the GRADEX rows resolve to the vector seal -- proving both triage outputs and both image columns land in the deliverable. Long names exercise the auto-fit name frame.

outputs.name: SlabVault_CompCards_perSlab_x6.pdf
outputs.spec: Exactly six press-ready 89 x 127 mm portrait consignment comp-cards -- ONE single-record card per roster row (page-count = row-count = 6) -- exported from the one-file-per-row InDesign data-merge with 3 mm bleed and crop marks at ~300 DPI; each card binds its PlayerName/SetYear/Grade/CertNo/AskPrice verbatim from the roster, drops that slab's neutralized, white-background packshot into the 60 x 84 mm photo window (>=709 x 992 px so it prints >=300 DPI), and drops the correct prepped grading seal into the 24 x 24 mm seal window (flat vector gradex_seal.svg for GRADEX rows, transparent-ground holographic raster apex_seal.png for APEX rows). THE OWNED DESIGNED ENDPOINT.

outputs.name: packshots_on_white_x6
outputs.spec: Six slab packshots, each neutralized to its in-frame grey card then lifted off the cluttered table onto flat pure-white (#FFFFFF) with no drop shadow and no grey gradient, the wood grain / charger / coffee ring / grey card all gone, each centered and cropped/resized to the 60 x 84 mm (5:7) photo-window ratio at ONE consistent fill-scale with even margin (so a small vintage slab and a tall modern slab read the same size in the storefront grid) and kept at >=709 x 992 px. Accompanied by a report of the final white-balance and exposure move AND the final pixel dimensions of each frame. Grey card is EXCLUDED from these delivered crops (grade card-neutrality on the retained masters below, not here).

outputs.name: neutralized_masters_cardbearing_x6
outputs.spec: Six retained neutralized master frames, one per slab, with the physical 18% grey card STILL IN FRAME -- the artifact on which card-neutrality is graded (each card driven to a clean neutral, the whole set matched to one shared white point and exposure feel while staying true-to-colour). Retained precisely because the delivered packshots crop the card out; grey-card tolerance is checked here, card-exclusion is checked on the packshots separately.

outputs.name: grading_seals_prepped
outputs.spec: The two grading-partner seals prepped triage-correct: gradex_seal.svg as clean vector line art traced only after crop-to-bounds + crisp prep, and apex_seal.png as the photographed holographic hologram cropped and knocked to transparency then kept as a high-resolution raster (>=283 px square) -- NOT vectorized, so the foil sheen survives to print.

connector_workflow.note: SL-01 (cool blue window light, flat): WARM the temperature and nudge tint until the in-frame 18% grey card reads neutral (R=G=B), then lift exposure/contrast slightly so the card sits at mid-grey and the slab reads true. Reason the exact temp/tint/exposure to THIS card by eye -- do NOT reuse another frame's numbers -- and REPORT the move. Single primitive-built adjustments call (replaces the deprecated image_adjust_color_temperature / _highlights / _brightness_and_contrast / _vibrance_and_saturation). This output is the retained card-bearing master for SL-01.

Knock SL-01 onto flat pure-white via remove_background with options.backgroundColor='#FFFFFF' -- the tool-sanctioned single-call 'product on clean white' path. This lifts the slab as the foreground and removes the wood table, charger, coffee ring AND the grey card in one pass; flat white, no shadow, no gradient. Deliberately NOT select_subject -> invert_selection -> image_fill_area (fill_area solids the mask flat and is the wrong path).

Center the slab (focus:subject) and crop/resize to the 60 x 84 mm (5:7) photo-window ratio at the SHARED batch fill-scale with even margin, holding the result at >=709 x 992 px so it clears the 300 DPI print floor. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only, never generative-expand / never upscale. REPORT final px. Consistent fill-scale across all six is a gated decision -- this slab must not read larger or smaller than the others in the grid.

SL-02 (warm tungsten, dark): this frame must move the OPPOSITE direction from SL-01 -- COOL the temperature and LIFT exposure/shadows until its grey card reads neutral and it matches the shared white point. Adaptive: the batch is not uniformly cool, so a blanket 'warm everything' pass fails here. REPORT the move. Retained card-bearing master for SL-02.
Knock SL-02 onto flat pure-white via remove_background({backgroundColor:'#FFFFFF'}); table, charger, coffee ring and grey card removed. Same anti-pattern avoidance as step 2 (never fill_area).

Center and crop/resize the SMALL vintage slab to the 5:7 photo window at the SAME shared fill-scale as SL-01, even margin, >=709 x 992 px. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only. The consistency trap: a small physical slab naively cropped tight will read oversized versus the modern slabs -- match the fill-scale, not the frame. REPORT final px.

SL-03 (greenish fluorescent AND under-exposed): the dominant colour move is on TINT (push toward magenta to kill the green) while neutralizing the grey card, PLUS a real exposure lift -- a two-axis problem, not a simple temperature slide. Land the card neutral on the shared white point. REPORT the move. Retained card-bearing master for SL-03.
Knock SL-03 (reflective chrome refractor) onto flat pure-white via remove_background({backgroundColor:'#FFFFFF'}); the chrome glare and busy table are handled by the cutout. Never fill_area.
Center and crop/resize SL-03 to the 5:7 photo window at the shared fill-scale, even margin, >=709 x 992 px. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only. REPORT final px.

SL-04 (over-exposed near-daylight with hot highlights): PULL exposure/highlights/whites DOWN to recover the blown plastic case first, THEN a small WB nudge so its grey card lands neutral on the shared white point. Tonal recovery dominates here -- the opposite tonal problem to the dark frames. REPORT the move. Retained card-bearing master for SL-04.
Knock SL-04 onto flat pure-white via remove_background({backgroundColor:'#FFFFFF'}); table and grey card removed. Never fill_area.
Center and crop/resize SL-04 to the 5:7 photo window at the shared fill-scale, even margin, >=709 x 992 px. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only. REPORT final px.

SL-05 (strong cool blue open-shade AND dark): warm STRONGLY and lift shadows/exposure to bring it up while neutralizing its grey card to the shared white point; protect the card face from going muddy. The BIGGEST correction in the set -- proof that identical batch numbers cannot serve every frame. REPORT the move. Retained card-bearing master for SL-05.
Knock SL-05 onto flat pure-white via remove_background({backgroundColor:'#FFFFFF'}); table, charger and grey card removed. Never fill_area.
Center and crop/resize SL-05 to the 5:7 photo window at the shared fill-scale, even margin, >=709 x 992 px. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only. REPORT final px.

SL-06 (near-neutral, slightly warm and dull): its grey card is already close to neutral, so only a SMALL WB nudge is needed -- over-correcting pushes it off the set. The real work is tonal: add a modest contrast/clarity lift to match the set's feel without clipping. REPORT the (small WB, tonal) move. Frames now share one white point, each neutralized to its own grey card. Retained card-bearing master for SL-06.
Knock SL-06 onto flat pure-white via remove_background({backgroundColor:'#FFFFFF'}); table and grey card removed. Never fill_area.

Center and crop/resize the TALL modern SL-06 to the 5:7 photo window at the SAME shared fill-scale as the small vintage SL-02, even margin, >=709 x 992 px. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only. Completes the consistent-scale six-image set. REPORT final px.

Triage path A: the GRADEX seal is flat two-colour printed line art, so it CAN become clean vector. Prep-before-trace step 1: crop the oversized/off-centre export to the tight bounds of the seal so the trace sees only the mark, not the margin.
Prep-before-trace step 2: push contrast and set the black/white points so the two solid colours separate hard-edged -- a soft or low-contrast raster traces into ragged, doubled edges.
Trace the prepared flat GRADEX seal into a clean SVG so it stays razor-sharp at the 24 mm seal window across every GRADEX-graded comp-card.

Triage DIVERGES here: the APEX seal is a PHOTOGRAPH of a holographic tamper-proof hologram -- full of gradients and specular sheen -- so it CANNOT become clean line art (vectorizing it returns a flat muddy silhouette and kills the hologram). Crop only to the tight bounds of the seal; do NOT send it to image_vectorize.

Knock the dark surround to transparency so only the holographic APEX seal remains, keeping every gradient and highlight intact. remove_background -> transparency (NOT select->invert->fill, NOT a solid fill). This preserves the foil the vector path would have destroyed.

Square-crop/resize the transparent holographic seal to the 24 x 24 mm (1:1) seal-window ratio at >=283 px square so it prints >=300 DPI. Kept as a high-resolution raster placed via @Seal for the APEX rows. onSubjectClipping='extract', downscale-only.

connector_workflow.inputs_from: packshot_sl01_final, packshot_sl02_final, packshot_sl03_final, packshot_sl04_final, packshot_sl05_final, packshot_sl06_final, sl01_neutralized, sl02_neutralized, sl03_neutralized, sl04_neutralized, sl05_neutralized, sl06_neutralized, gradex_seal.svg, apex_seal.png
connector_workflow.note: Initialize an upload session for the six white-background packshots, the six retained card-bearing neutralized masters, and the two prepped grading seals so the merge can resolve the packshots and seals by the @Packshot and @Seal columns. Packshots uploaded under the exact names the roster references. (Plumbing.)
Finalize the upload; returns the asset URNs the roster's @Packshot / @Seal columns resolve to for each slab's single-record comp-card. (Plumbing.)

One-file-per-row InDesign data-merge: bind each of the six roster rows (PlayerName/SetYear/Grade/CertNo/AskPrice) into the authored SINGLE-RECORD .indd's live <<fields>> and drop that row's neutralized packshot into the @Packshot frame AND its mapped grading seal into the @Seal frame -- producing EXACTLY ONE merged comp-card per row (six cards); the auto-fit name frame shrinks long player names. [T] requires the hand-authored template. A convert_pdf_to_indd template or a multi-up sheet would not bind / cannot be produced -- this is the corrected merge path. document_merge_data_vector is the WRONG tool (text-only, cannot bind the two image columns).

Export the merged single-record comp-cards to a press-ready ~300 DPI 89 x 127 mm + 3 mm bleed PDF with crop marks, one card per slab. Acceptance: page-count = row-count = 6; if fewer, the merge collapsed rows and failed.

chaining_note: Strict output-to-input chaining throughout. Six per-slab sub-chains fan out from the raw slab photos, each an image_apply_adjustments neutralization (adaptive per frame: warm+lift the cool flat SL-01, cool+lift the warm dark SL-02, magenta-tint+lift the green/dark SL-03, tonally recover the over-exposed SL-04, strongly warm+lift the deep-shade dark SL-05, hold WB but add tone on the near-neutral SL-06) that becomes the RETAINED card-bearing master, followed by image_remove_background({backgroundColor:'#FFFFFF'}) that lifts the slab onto flat white and removes the table AND the grey card, followed by image_crop_and_resize that centers to the 5:7 photo window at ONE shared fill-scale and holds >=709 x 992 px -- every neutralization driven to that frame's own in-frame 18% grey card so all six converge on one shared white point, and every crop matched to one fill-scale so the slabs do not jump size in the grid. The two grading seals TRIAGE into two paths: the flat GRADEX seal runs crop_to_bounds -> crisp adjustments -> image_vectorize into a clean SVG (19->20->21), while the photographed holographic APEX seal diverges to crop_to_bounds -> image_remove_background (transparency) -> crop_and_resize into a high-res transparent raster (22->23->24), deliberately never touching image_vectorize. The six final packshots, the six retained masters and the two prepped seals converge into the upload session(25) -> finalize(26) -> document_merge_data_layout(27), which also consumes the authored single-record .indd and the roster CSV and emits one merged comp-card per row, resolving BOTH @Packshot and @Seal per row. The merged set is exported to the per-slab press PDF(28). Nothing after the raw loads originates outside the chain.
difficulty_rationale: Long-horizon flagship rebuilt from the killed one-recipe-six-times version: 28 connector calls, 9 distinct Adobe tools across three groups (image_* grading/cutout/prep/vectorize, asset_* storage, document_* merge/export), above the >=10 call / >=6 distinct-tool floor even after stripping the 2 upload steps. hardness_rationale: FAILURE GATE: the agent trips on WRONG DECISIONS, not a self-measurement. (1) Per-frame divergent white-balance/exposure by eye -- every slab carries a physical 18% grey card and the acceptance criterion is that each finished card reads a clean neutral with the whole set matched to one white point; the six frames were lit in DIFFERENT directions (cool, warm, green, over-exposed, deep-shade, near-neutral) so pushing one uniform correction through all six visibly mismatches the set, and the agent must REPORT the WB/exposure move it applied per frame (it knows it because it set it -- never a measured pixel readout). (2) A two-way triage of the two grading seals that require DIFFERENT correct treatments -- the flat GRADEX seal prepped-and-vectorized to clean line art, the photographed holographic APEX seal knocked to transparency and kept as high-res raster because a trace would flatten its hologram; getting it wrong is invisible in a thumbnail and only shows when the APEX cards print dead. HUMAN-HARD ELEMENTS: (a) cross-asset neutralization of six differently-lit slab photos to a common white point, each needing its own opposite-direction correction; (b) a numeric consistent-fill-scale + >=709 x 992 px print-DPI gate across a small vintage slab and a tall modern slab so they do not jump size in the storefront grid; (c) the seal triage. TRAP (NOT disclosed in the brief as a defect): the APEX holographic seal looks like 'just another grading seal', so the naive path sends both seals through the same crop->vectorize pipeline; vectorizing the hologram returns a flat muddy silhouette that passes as a thumbnail but destroys the foil at print, while the correct path routes only the flat GRADEX seal to image_vectorize and takes the APEX one through remove_background-to-transparency. A second pitfall sits in the grade (identical batch numbers on six differently-lit frames leave the set mismatched) and a third in the scale (cropping each slab tight to its own frame makes the small slab read oversized). MEASURABLE ACCEPTANCE (grader-side, on the outputs): every grey card neutral within +-3 levels on the RETAINED card-bearing masters and the set on one white point with per-frame WB/exposure reported; every packshot on flat #FFFFFF at one consistent fill-scale and >=709 x 992 px with final px reported and the grey card excluded; the two grading seals prepped triage-correct (one clean vector, one transparent-ground raster >=283 px square); and exactly one press-ready ~300 DPI 89 x 127 mm comp-card per roster row.
